Findings: Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary:  An enrollee has requested self-injectable testosterone injection (cypionate) for treatment of his medical condition.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that there is sufficient support for the requested medication in this clinical setting.  Low testosterone can lead to complications including reduced libido/erectile dysfunction, reduced muscle mass and strength, increased adiposity, osteoporosis/low bone mass, depressed mood and fatigue.  For these reasons, many providers treat patients with hypogonadism when their testosterone level is less than 350 ng/dL.  The general target level for testosterone ranges from 350 to 750 ng/dL, which is roughly the range for healthy, androgen-sufficient adult men. Testosterone levels should be monitored three to six months after initiation of treatment in order to assure that the patient’s testosterone level is optimal and the dose of testosterone replacement therapy should be adjusted accordingly.  This patient has clinical and biochemical evidence of hypogonadism and is likely to benefit from testosterone replacement therapy.  Therefore, self-injectable testosterone injection (cypionate) is medically indicated for the treatment of this patient. Applying the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) guidelines, in the absence of daily skilled therapy needs, SNF services are not considered medically necessary. A patient who does not require hands on support for walking or transfers is able to do daily exercise without support from a therapist. There is no expectation that this patient’s course of rehabilitation will change as his surgical procedure was uncomplicated as was his rehabilitation thus far (Ward, et al). The patient had reached a level of function that did not require daily skilled therapy to restore or maintain function. Continued progress can be achieved with continued exercise without daily supervision from a skilled therapist. Further, there were no daily skilled nursing needs. Daily skilled services are not necessary to restore or maintain function. The patient did not require SNF services to establish a safe and effective maintenance program. For these reasons, the SNF services provided from the dates indicated were not medically necessary for treatment of this patient’s medical condition.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: An 18-year-old male enrollee requested three hours per day of inpatient rehabilitation services for medical treatment of his multiple fractures.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. According to the documentation submitted for review, this patient has significant functional loss, is willing to participate in therapy, and does not have acute medical issues interfering with rehabilitation. He requires multiple therapies coordinating together such as physical therapy, occupational therapy, and with his history of brain injury, access to speech/language therapy and/or neuropsychological therapy. Dahm and Ponsford note that traumatic orthopedic injury and traumatic brain injury, both of which the patient has, place an individual at risk for long-term disability and impairment of socialization. As such, intensive therapies in a highly monitored setting such as inpatient rehabilitation can reduce the risk of these adverse outcomes. In this patient’s case, three hours per day of inpatient rehabilitation services at the frequency of five days per week is medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition.

Findings: A 34-year-old female enrollee has requested physical therapy and occupational therapy for treatment of her status post cerebral hemorrhage. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that review of the submitted documentation and relevant literature fails to demonstrate the medical necessity of the requested therapy. Acute stroke care includes cerebral reperfusion interventions when appropriate, addressing hemodynamic issues, secondary stroke prophylaxis, various supportive management strategies and preventing complications such as aspiration and deep venous thromboses (Adams, et al). Functional impairments due to acquired brain insults such as stroke can improve with time, such as natural recovery processes (Turner-Stokes, et a), but are also amenable to rehabilitation interventions. In this case, the patient sustained an acute stroke with significant functional impairments.  She has been undergoing inpatient rehabilitation, and has made significant progress. The physical and occupational therapy notes submitted for review demonstrates that she has plateaued with respect to her function. She is ambulating about 80 feet at moderate assistance. She continues to require contact guard to minimum assistance for dressing and moderate assistance for toileting. Based on the documentation submitted for review, further physical therapy and occupational therapy services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 20-year-old female enrollee has requested residential treatment for treatment of her behavioral health condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the submitted documentation fails to demonstrate the medical necessity of the services at issue.  Modern psychiatric practice is aimed at treating individuals in the least restrictive setting to consolidate treatment gains and foster autonomy, resilience and mental wellness.  In this patient’s case, substance use was problematic but the patient had not pursued specialty care at a less restrictive setting during this episode, such as intensive outpatient or partial hospitalization with augmentative 12-step programming in the community.  Upon presentation, the patient was motivated for treatment services.  She was not experiencing a withdrawal syndrome, and she was sleeping well.  The patient had mood symptoms, but these symptoms appeared to be related to her drug use, family stress and bereavement.  She was not diagnosed with a distinct affective disorder, and she did not have an acute psychiatric syndrome.  Per the medical records, the patient did not pose an imminent risk danger to self or others due to her depression.  While admitted, the patient was started on naltrexone, an opioid receptor antagonist used to treat opioid use disorders.  This medication helps particularly with craving and does not require a 24-hour supervised setting for initiation and titration.  Additionally, she was not having difficulty maintaining her self-care or activities of daily living.  The patient had a stable home environment.  Finally, the documentation provided did not offer a rationale supporting the clinical need for residential placement as opposed to treatment at a lower level of care.  All told, residential treatment provided from the time period specified was not medically indicated for the treatment of this patient.

Further, the services were reasonably expected to improve the patient’s condition and prevent a more serious episode of illness. Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of an 18-year-old female enrollee has requested long-term in home licensed vocational nurse (LVN) nursing care for treatment of the enrollee’s cerebral palsy.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the submitted documentation and relevant literature demonstrates the medical necessity of the requested services. This patient presents with cerebral palsy and multiple sequelae, including poor airway protection, ADHD, anxiety/panic attacks, and dysphagia necessitating gastrostomy tube feedings. These medical conditions mandate constant skilled supervision with expertise to provide timely intervention. She is dependent for airway clearance, requiring direction for self-suctioning during the day and caregiver suctioning while she sleeps (approximately 10 hours each night). She must be monitored for aspiration events, with skilled interventions if necessary, such as chest physiotherapy, breathing treatments, and supplemental oxygen. Her ability to perform activities of daily living is severely limited by her diagnoses, and she requires support in all areas in order to maintain health and well-being. The mother recently passed away, and the father is a full-time professional that is unable to provide her care at home. Therefore, the patient requires trained nursing to maintain airway clearance, with the goal of preventing future episodes of aspiration pneumonia, respiratory distress syndrome, and need for tracheostomy. Further, she needs to be monitored for anxiety so that timely intervention is possible. Therefore, long-term in home licensed vocational nurse (LVN) nursing care is medically necessary and appropriate. Therefore, based on the medical literature cited above and the documentation submitted for review, the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition.

As such, the requested skilled nursing services are not medically necessary.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: A 37-year-old male enrollee has requested home health care.  for treatment of his paraplegia.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the submitted documentation fails to demonstrate the medical necessity of the requested services in this patient’s case.  Patients with spinal cord injury are at high risk for pressure ulcers.  In addition, once formed, pressure ulcers can be difficult to heal due to metabolic and physiological changes in the tissues below the level of the spinal cord injury.  With respect to treatment, the key areas of focus remain ongoing appropriate pressure relief, optimizing nutrition, modifying behavioral factors such as smoking, and promoting an optimal wound environment.  In this case, the patient has multiple chronic wounds that have reportedly persisted for years despite extensive home health services.  He does not have any documented impairments that would be expected to preclude his ability to complete his wound care independently with an appropriate set up and training.  Home nursing notes document that he is able to perform his wound care.  The patient is not homebound and can follow-up in a wound care center for intermittent debridements, as needed.  All told, the requested home health care is not medically indicated for the treatment of this patient.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 19-year-old female has requested past and prospective coverage for inpatient psychiatric treatment of her behavioral health issues.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that inpatient psychiatric care is aimed at decompressing the acute exacerbations of episodic serious mental illness. This patient presented as a distressed, mentally ill patient.  The patient’s records throughout the hospitalization demonstrate the patient could have been safely and effectively treated in a less restrictive setting as of the date in question. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) recommends the “psychiatrist should determine the least restrictive setting for treatment that will be most likely not only to address the patient’s safety, but also to promote improvement in the patient’s condition. The determination of an appropriate setting for treatment should include consideration of the patient’s symptom severity, co-occurring psychiatric or general medical conditions, available support system, and level of functioning”. Although acute hospitalization was appropriate to fully treat this high risk patient, the medical records fail to justify the necessity of inpatient acute care through a date at issue. Specifically, the extent of psychotropic medication management did not necessitate the inpatient setting. Further, the acute suicidality that justified the admission had resolved per both physician and nursing documentation. The psychiatrist noted that the patient was a little less depressed and not suicidal, psychotic or cognitively impaired with a better form of thought. Nursing commented that the patient was “feeling better”, “visible in the milieu”, and denied suicidal ideation. The patient posed no imminent threat to self or others and was not gravely disabled due to her psychiatric illness. However, she remained symptomatic and treatment in an intermediate setting, such as residential services specializing in evidence-based psychotherapies for patients PTSD and eating disorders was indicated to consolidate her treatment gains, reduce morbidity and lessen the chance of re-admission. Based on the documentation provided, and review of relevant medical relevant literature, discharge to a less restrictive treatment setting such as outpatient therapy on the date at issue would have been safe, reasonable, and consistent with the APA treatment guidelines. Thus, the services provided from the date at issue, and forward were not and are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: A 34-year-old female has requested intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) home therapy for treatment of multiple sclerosis.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the patient has a history of multiple sclerosis with recent exacerbation and is breast feeding. She has been on platform medications in the past. Treatment with interferon is not advisable during breastfeeding, per the prescribing information. It is not known if Copaxone is excreted in breast milk. It is also not known if IVIG is excreted in breast milk. However, a recent review of seven randomized trials evaluating IVIG for relapsing-remitting MS supports the use of IVIG and a consensus statement indicated, “For women with relapsing-remitting MS who are pregnant or breastfeeding, the panel agreed it is reasonable to consider IVIG as a treatment option.” (Feasby, et al.) Therefore, there is indication of need for treatment in this patient’s case, and IVIG represents a medically reasonable treatment option until the patient’s platform medications such as Rebif and Avonex can be resumed.

Findings: A 48-year-old male has requested coverage for a past stay and a continued stay for post-acute inpatient rehabilitation for treatment of his medical condition. The standard care for patients with post-traumatic memory, judgment, and cognitive impairments includes multi-disciplinary therapies, including occupational therapy, speech therapy, and physical therapy as appropriate, to facilitate safety and recovery to an optimal level of independence. Appropriate level of care varies per patient, and needs to address safety, level of in-home support, and strategies for community integration. These services can be provided as an outpatient at the day treatment level. Literature shows that with intensive therapies, rate of recovery may be more rapid, but does not show that ultimate degree of recovery is improved. In addition, there is lack of evidence that overall inpatient or outpatient care is preferable in facilitating recovery after brain injury. Thus, with appropriate supervision, and in the absence of significant behavioral or mobility issues that would make outpatient rehabilitation unsafe, the patient should be considered for a day treatment program as an outpatient.

The key to acute stroke care includes cerebral reperfusion interventions when appropriate, addressing hemodynamic issues, secondary stroke prophylaxis, various supportive management strategies, and preventing complications such as aspiration and deep venous thromboses (Adams, et al). Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The conservator of a 21-year-old male enrollee has requested for an inpatient, post-acute traumatic brain injury program for physical, occupational, speech and vocational therapies for treatment of the enrollee status post traumatic brain injury. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the standard care for patients with post-traumatic memory, judgment, and cognitive impairments includes multi-disciplinary therapies such as occupational therapy, speech therapy and physical therapy as appropriate, in order to facilitate safety and recovery to an optimal level of independence. The appropriate level of care is often patient specific and should include considerations of the patient’s level of safety, level of in-home support and strategies for community integration. The literature demonstrates that patient care in comparable cases is often best provided in a structured, inpatient setting. The peer reviewed medical literature has also demonstrated that recovery rates are often better in young adults, than in older individuals. In this case, the patient’s records indicate ongoing improvements, which can be anticipated to continue with appropriate future treatment. All told, ongoing care in an inpatient, post-acute traumatic brain injury program is appropriate and medically necessary.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of an 11-year-old male enrollee has requested authorization and coverage for Hizentra, 30 grams per month, divided into weekly doses for treatment of the enrollee’s immunodeficiency.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that review of the submitted clinical information does not demonstrate the patient meets accepted clinical indications for Hizentra (immune globulin) at this time. The patient’s specific immunoglobulin levels showed a two to four fold increase post vaccination and his IgG levels appear to be within the normal range. In the absence of evidence of abnormal IgG levels, treatment with immune globulin is not supported. If future pneumococcal antibody titers demonstrate that the patient’s titers are not maintained, then the request for Hizentra should be reconsidered. Based upon the evidence provided, it is unlikely that Hizentra would be of any benefit at this time. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial was appropriate in this case.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Treatment Sub Category: Inpatient Transfer to Lower Level of Care
Findings: A 23-year-old male enrollee has requested reimbursement and prospective authorization and coverage for continued skilled nursing level of care including physical, occupational, and speech therapy, from a specific date and forward.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that based on review of the available records, the patient is at a custodial level of care and does not require SNF level of care services. The records indicate that the patient has shown some very modest but largely inconsistent signs of progress, and is essentially in a minimally conscious state. He has not been tracking consistently or consistently following commands. He has been dependent for all care and mobility. Some ongoing recovery and functional progress may occur over the next 12-18 months, but the extent of rate of recovery is likely to be very slow given the severity of his injuries and the minimal progress that has been demonstrated since the initial accident. As such, further rehabilitative efforts can be provided at a lower level of care as no marginally significant improvement in health or functional outcomes is expected with ongoing SNF level care.  In the peer reviewed publications, Lombardi and colleagues’ literature review reported that, “there is no reliable evidence to support, or rule out, the effectiveness of multisensory programmes in patients in coma or vegetative state.” Similarly, a review by Meyer and colleagues on evidence-based interventions used to promote patient arousal from coma concluded that although each of the interventions showed promise and warrant further study, “More methodologically rigorous study is needed before any definitive conclusions can be drawn.” In addition, Georgiopoulos and colleagues noted that no therapeutic treatments were proven to be efficacious in significantly improving the recovery course or functional outcomes in the setting of vegetative state or minimally conscious state. Therefore, the requested multidisciplinary rehabilitative interventions including occupational, physical, and speech therapy is not medically necessary in lieu of care provided at a less intensive level such as custodial care with intermittent therapy services.  Consistent with these findings, the requested continued SNF care from the date in question and forward has not been shown to be medically necessary in the treatment of this patient’s medical condition.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of a 13-year-old female has requested coverage for 12 hours per day of in-home skilled nursing services for treatment of her functional quadriplegia.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that according to the American Academy of Pediatrics Guidelines for Home Care of Infants, Children, and Adolescents with Chronic Disease, the goal of a home health care program for adolescents with chronic conditions is the provision of comprehensive health care within a nurturing home environment that maximizes the capabilities of the individual and minimizes the effects of the disabilities. In the case of this patient, she is a medically fragile adolescent with complex medical problems including uncontrolled seizures that place her at great risk for morbidity and even mortality. She feeds orally, but is considered by staff to be at high risk for aspiration, including pneumonia, particularly should she have a seizure while eating. Further, her musculoskeletal deformities place her at risk for skin breakdown and decubitus ulcer formation. Moreover, she has central sleep apnea and apnea with seizures, jeopardizing her respiratory status. In light of these medical issues, the level of care that the patient requires necessitates experience and attention to detail, with ability to rapidly intervene should difficulties arise. Her care is not custodial in nature. The patient requires 12 hours per day of in-home skilled nursing services to prevent complications and morbidity as a result of her complex medical problems.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 70-year-old female enrollee has requested for skilled nursing facility level of care with physical therapy and occupational therapy for treatment of her Guillain-Barre syndrome. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) has a generally favorable natural course and relatively good prognosis. There are standard treatment options that have demonstrated to be effective treatments for this condition (van Doorn, et al.). Despite the generally good prognosis and available therapeutic options, some patients continue to have significant functional impairments at six months or longer following the onset of symptoms. To date, highly intensive rehabilitation services have not been proven to effectuate better long-term functional outcomes in this setting (Khan, et al.). Further inpatient rehabilitation and skilled nursing facility level care including physical therapy and occupational therapy is not medically necessary. Rehabilitation services can be provided in the community setting. Further inpatient care would be custodial in nature based on the available records, and therefore not medically necessary.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: An 18-year-old male enrollee has requested reimbursement for Adolescent Mental Health Residential Treatment.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that on review of the patient’s psychiatric evaluation on admission to the RTC, he was described on MSE as being cooperative, well groomed, and calm, with a good sense of humor, logical thoughts and no current or acute suicidal or homicidal ideation. The provider also noted that the patient was motivated for treatment. Progress notes dated four days later describe full affect, no auditory or visual hallucinations, and no suicidal or homicidal ideation. Six days from the progress notes referenced above, the patient’s mood was described as stable and on the next day the provider noted a bright affect with no suicidal or homicidal ideation. Five days from the previous entry, it was noted that the patient was socializing with peers and was compliant with treatment. Based on the Child and Adolescent Level of Care Utilization System (CALOCUS) criteria and the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP) treatment guidelines, this patient was a candidate for a less restrictive level of care during the period under review. These guidelines recommend treatment in the least restrictive setting possible, and given this patient’s symptoms, he would have been safely and adequately managed in an intensive outpatient program (IOP). For these reasons, the medical necessity for residential level of care has not been established.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 54-year-old female enrollee has requested continued physical therapy and rehabilitation in the skilled nursing facility for treatment of her status post hemorrhagic cerebrovascular accident.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that this patient has a high baseline level of function, including living independently in the community, ambulating without an assistive device, driving and working.  She had profound acute changes to her functional status due to a hemorrhagic stroke.  She has been making slow, but fairly steady, progress while at the skilled nursing facility.  The distances she is ambulating and the level of assistance needed for ambulation have been improving steadily.  Her ability to transfer and perform self-care has been improving. This patient would have been expected to make further functional progress from the said date forward based on her progress up to that date and her high baseline functional status.  Stroke is a condition that is amenable to natural recovery and therapy interventions.  These expected functional gains would be clinically meaningful.  While these gains would not likely eliminate the need for care, they would be expected to significantly improve the patient’s independence. All told, continued physical therapy and rehabilitation in the skilled nursing facility during this timeframe was and is medically indicated for the treatment of this patient.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 64-year-old female enrollee has requested skilled nursing facility (SNF) services (including occupational therapy and physical therapy)  for treatment of her medical condition status post ischemic stroke.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that in the present case, the patient sustained an acute brain stem stroke and has become severely debilitated in comparison to her baseline status of living alone independently in the community, driving and working. She has made significant progress since her initial stroke, but these improvements have largely been limited to the domains of speech and swallowing. Despite ongoing inpatient therapy care, her self-care and mobility have remained at close to total assistance. As of the said date, she was still requiring multiple person assistance for getting to a stand position, had poor standing balance, and was dependent for transfers. She was non-ambulatory and not making any documented progress with wheelchair mobility. She had already been upgraded to a regular diet and thin liquids, which she was tolerating without signs of aspiration and was no longer in need of inpatient level speech therapy services. There were no documented ongoing skilled nursing needs such as complex wound care, initiation of self-care related to enteral feeding or ostomy care, or medical needs requiring ongoing inpatient care. Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 33-year-old female enrollee has requested treatment at an acute rehabilitation center for treatment of her traumatic brain injury.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the medical literature indicates that efforts at rehabilitation are most effective early after an injury (Turner-Stokes, et al). This level of care was provided to this patient in the sub-acute rehabilitation facility. All told, she will likely continue to make progress but her pattern indicates that it will be gradual and may take years. Her rate of brain recovery will prevent her from making substantial gains with an inpatient rehabilitation program. Her rate of progress will be at least as good if not better at home with community based programs. Rehabilitation allows a person to maximize the gains available but does not increase the rate of brain healing. Overall, it is the severity of the injury not the site of the patient’s care that is predictive of outcome (Anderson, et al). As such, specialty care for general rehabilitation goals has not been shown to substantially improve patient recovery in this clinical circumstance. For these reasons, the medical necessity of the requested services has not been established in the treatment of this patient’s medical condition.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The spouse of a deceased female enrollee has requested 24-hour in-home nursing care services for treatment of the enrollee's medical condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that at issue in this case is whether a prudent layperson in the patient’s circumstances would believe he or she was experiencing an emergency medical condition or urgent medical condition for four months. Upon review of the submitted documentation, a prudent layperson would not have believed he or she was experiencing an ongoing emergent situation for four months. Therefore, these services do not meet prudent layperson criteria for an emergency medical condition. However, there can be the possibility of imminent death especially in terminally ill patients with cancer and these patients may require palliative care. Based upon the documentation provided, this patient appeared to be quite ill upon discharge from the hospital. She had a very poor performance status. This would have precluded travel back to the in-Plan service area for palliative care. Although there is not a clear clinical description of the patient’s performance status or respiratory status, it appears she did experience a significant deterioration of her medical condition while out of the country. A prudent layperson in this patient’s circumstances would reasonably expect that the worsening of her symptoms constituted an urgent medical situation which precluded travel back to the in-Plan service area.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The representative of a 47-year-old male enrollee has requested skilled nursing care services for treatment of the enrollee’s medical condition status post intracerebral hemorrhage.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that this patient has experienced a devastating stroke of high severity. It is expected he will remain dependent. However, he has experienced a hemorrhagic stroke. Outcome for hemorrhagic stroke in a patient under 50 years of age is highly varied. Predicting outcome after a hemorrhagic stroke in this patient population is not a highly reliable exercise because progress in therapy may not be as limited as it is under other circumstances and because the degree and rate of brain healing is highly varied. This patient has experienced a stroke of high severity with the expectation that he will remain dependent on his caregivers. The occupational, physical and speech therapy records provided for review demonstrate that he has only made minimal progress, has a severely reduced capacity to respond to therapy, and has achieved a functional plateau. All told, the patient is unable to progress with daily skilled therapy due to the severity of the brain injury and the expected rate of brain healing. Therefore, the services at issue have not been established as medically necessary in this patient’s care.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of a 14-year-old male enrollee has requested more than 4 hours per day of shift nursing care services and 8 hours per day of skilled nursing care for treatment of the enrollee’s myasthenia gravis. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that this patient has congenital myasthenia gravis (MG) with clinical symptoms significant enough to warrant the type of nursing care defined as “skilled”. Although the patient’s needs may not require acute or intensive care at this time, the concept behind skilled home nursing care is to prevent regression of his condition to the point where hospitalization is needed. This translates into best medical practice and the standard of care indicated for this patient is skilled nursing care from the said date and forward. The patient’s records clearly document the need for skilled nursing care in order to maintain a severely compromised airway. As noted by Hardy and Rittenberry of caring for patients with MG, “Nursing care is complex and involves patient education about drug therapy and treatment options as well as caring for the numerous problems that arise from varying degrees of muscle weakness”. The authors also found that, “Skilled nursing assessment and intervention can help protect the myasthenic patient from the life-threatening complications of respiratory compromise.” Thus, based on review of the literature and the details of this case, skilled nursing care was and is indeed medically necessary for this patient with congenital MG. The requested 8 hours of skilled nursing care per day have been shown to be medically necessary for this patient

Treatment Category: Home Health Care

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The spouse of a 72-year-old female enrollee has requested services at a skilled nursing facility (SNF) level of care for treatment of the enrollee’s Parkinson’s disease.   Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the patient sustained a right hip fracture. She underwent a prolonged rehabilitation process but was unable to maintain independence in regards to her self-care and mobility to a safe degree. She underwent another extensive period of inpatient rehabilitation during the said time frame related to her chronic debility and progressive Parkinson’s disease. While physical therapy and exercise are appropriate in the management of Parkinson's disease-related gait disorder (Ceravolo,), there should be a transition from an initial supervised period to an independent period where the patient takes on the responsibility of maintaining activity levels (Morris, et al). The patient in this case underwent a period of supervised therapy and was transitioned to a restorative nursing program.  Notably, she had been discharged from skilled therapies due to a plateau in progress.  The remainder of her stay during the said dates is not documented to have involved or required skilled therapy or skilled nursing interventions.  The patient was medically stable and followed by a physician on a routine basis as an outpatient.  There were no complex wounds requiring ongoing inpatient care. There were no ongoing skilled therapy needs. Additionally, there was no documentation of significant functional progress that was the result of additional skilled therapy interventions. As of the date in question and forward, the patient was receiving custodial level services for supporting her self-care, activities of daily living and mobility. Thus, the inpatient care in question was custodial in nature and not medically necessary.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 31-year-old male enrollee has requested continued skilled nursing facility (SNF) care including speech therapy, occupational therapy, and physical therapy for treatment of his primary lateral sclerosis.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that primary lateral sclerosis is a progressive degenerative neurological condition resulting in severe chronic disability. Without an effective agent to halt destruction of the neurons, patients generally continue to decline (Ropper and Samuels). Skilled therapy cannot halt the degenerative process (Dalbello-Haas and colleagues). From a review of the patient’s records, although he did show some progress with high dose steroid therapy, he was unable to continue to improve functionally. The patient’s provider described the patient as dependent in activities of daily living but noted that he did improve in his ability to feed himself. However, he did not improve in swallowing and was down-graded to thickened liquids. Overall, the records demonstrate the patient has only made minimal gains with skilled therapy and has not progressed with skilled physical therapy as of the date in question. While he requires daily exercise to maintain his current function, exercise can be provided in a variety of ways outside of the SNF setting. Given the patient’s underlying diagnosis and functional status as of the date at issue, the medical necessity of continued skilled services beyond the last authorized date of service has not been established.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 55-year-old male enrollee requested reimbursement for previous and authorization for prospective skilled nursing facility (SNF) services and/or skilled nursing facility rehabilitation services for treatment of his medical condition status post cerebral vascular accident (CVA). Findings: The physician reviewer found that in the medical literature there are limited studies on the outcomes for comprehensive programs in treating this patient population. The newer literature focuses on testing new techniques, but overall the data on patient outcome following a hemorrhagic stroke has been stable for over a decade. Essentially the research supports clear benefits of stroke rehabilitation with early intervention. There is little improvement with later treatment (Ronning and Guldvog). In addition, more than three months following a stroke, there were no substantial advancements in hospital versus settings (Anderson and colleagues). This patient’s stroke prevents him from clinically benefitting from daily skilled therapy. Therefore, the skilled nursing care at issue has not been established as medically necessary for treatment of this patient’s condition.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 54-year-old male enrollee has requested skilled nursing services for treatment of his following multiple ischemic strokes.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that review of the submitted clinical documentation demonstrates that SNF level of care was medically appropriate and necessary from the date in question to the present. Further, the patient continues to require rehabilitation care at a SNF level at this time. His functional progress has been impeded by behavioral issues which are improving with medication adjustments. He is now transferring with contact guard/minimal assistance and ambulates with minimal/moderate assistance level. His activities of daily living require moderate assistance and cueing. The patient’s cognitive skills are slowly improving, although he is agitated and impulsive at times. The patient has continued medical issues which require skilled nursing. His INR is not yet stable and requires daily adjustment. He remains at high risk for aspiration and dehydration without close monitoring. As such, it is appropriate to continue SNF level rehabilitation for three weeks from the date of this decision. At that time, the patient should be re-assessed so that a determination can be made concerning the patient’s ability to be discharged to an alternate level of care.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of a five-year-old male enrollee has requested skilled nursing services eight hours per day for treatment of the enrollee’s multiple medical conditions.   Findings:  The physician reviewer found that this patient is medically fragile with very complex medical problems and the potential for severe decompensation. He requires round-the-clock diligence to prevent the myriad of complications that could occur. He has been assessed with chronic lung disease and reactive airway disease and requires aggressive pulmonary care, including frequent suctioning, breathing treatments, and Vest therapy. He also occasionally requires supplemental oxygen. He is at increased risk for aspiration because of gastroesophageal reflux and intractable seizures, and has been hospitalized multiple times with this diagnosis. While trained unskilled caregivers can safely administer routine enteral medications and feedings, only caregivers with professional training and expertise can detect subtle changes in respiratory status and respond with appropriate adaptations to the treatment regimen, thus preventing progression to more severe respiratory compromise. In addition, this patient requires frequent suctioning, medication administration, skin care, and therapeutic manipulations.This level of care requires experience and attention to detail so that needs are met, problems recognized promptly, and treatment administered in a timely fashion. While trained family members are often capable of assisting with care of children with this degree of complexity, skilled nursing is essential to provide adequate care. As such, I find that the skilled home nursing services the patient received during this period of time were medically appropriate and necessary for this patient. Furthermore, the submitted documentation demonstrates the patient continues to require this level of care, and therefore, the request for ongoing skilled nursing services at a frequency of eight hours per day is medically necessary.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 54-year-old male enrollee has requested for post acute skilled physical, occupational, and speech therapies as well as residential care, behavior modification and psychotherapy counseling for treatment following multiple ischemic strokes.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that from a review of the available records, it appears that the patient has significant functional deficits at one year post-stroke. These outcomes were predictable based upon his status in the early stages post-stroke and in the rehabilitation phases of his illness (Ovbiagele, et al). Further, he has not gained significantly since his discharge from a skilled facility (Kwakkel, et al). At this juncture, the records indicate that he has reached a functional plateau (Heuschmann, et al). The patient continues with neglect of his left side, impulsiveness, and agitation with new information and he is also on a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube. Based on a review of the relevant medical literature, additional gains are not expected or predicted as stroke rehabilitation cannot influence outcome in the absence of continued brain healing. As such, the services at issue have not been demonstrated to be medically necessary in this clinical setting and the denial was therefore appropriate.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of a 12-year-old female enrollee has requested skilled nursing facility (SNF) services for treatment of the enrollee’s grand mal seizures (poorly controlled) and developmental delays. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that in treating patients with epilepsy, the delivery of high-quality care is complicated by the complexity and diversity of symptoms. Overall, epilepsy has a pervasive impact on the lives of patients with intellectual disabilities and occurs more frequently in this patient population. Children and adolescents offer unique challenges as they are more likely to suffer lifelong intractable epilepsy with multiple seizure types. In addition, the younger patients often cannot clearly express their complaints about antiepileptic drug (AED) side effects, and the caregiver’s role becomes crucial as the patient’s advocate. Patients who have both epilepsy and intellectual disability have significant problems requiring skilled health care management. Clinical nurse specialists have the unique opportunity to work with these patients and their families to help them develop self-management and family management skills. Given this patient’s specialized needs, the requested skilled nursing care should be provided to better to provide her an optimal quality of life. Further, this skilled nursing care will prevent complications from the patient’s intractable epilepsy during this vulnerable time in the patient’s current situation. Moreover, the Health Plan’s criteria defining medical necessity for skilled nursing services provides care for an acute exacerbation of a chronic medical condition. Thus, it is therefore reasonable to extend these benefits to a minor patient who requires the care of a caregiver who is unable to provide such services due to an acute condition affecting the abilities of the caregiver to administer such care. Accordingly, the requested skilled nursing care should be provided this patient until such time that the primary care giver is capable of providing her care.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 44-year-old male enrollee has requested post-acute inpatient cognitive rehabilitation for treatment of his status post traumatic brain injury.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the records indicate that the patient sustained multiple major injuries due to a motor vehicle accident, including traumatic brain injury and fractures of the face, axial skeleton and ribs. He has undergone acute inpatient rehabilitation and has made significant functional progress since the accident. He is off of respiratory support. The patient is stable on an oral diet. He is independent with his mobility. He is independent to supervision for his activities of daily living. He has been discharged to the community with family.Despite this progress, the patient continues to have residual cognitive deficits. He does require some ongoing rehabilitation services going forward.  The records, however, do not support the need for post-acute inpatient cognitive rehabilitation services at this time.  Currently, the research in the field of cognitive rehabilitation after acquired brain dysfunction does not permit firm conclusions regarding efficacy.  Methodologically weak literature, such as observational papers without control groups, have suggested some benefits to various cognitive therapy interventions, but have failed to discern treatment effect from natural improvements due to continued healing. In the sparse literature that has utilized relatively rigorous methodology, cognitive therapy interventions have not been demonstrated to have a significant, sustained effect on long-term functional outcomes over basic education, home cognitive exercises, reassurance, and the passage of time, as noted by Cicerone and colleagues. Overall, there are no realistic goals for the proposed readmission to acute inpatient rehabilitation stay that could not alternatively be met with rehabilitation services provided at a less intense setting, such as outpatient rehabilitation. All told, the requested post-acute inpatient cognitive rehabilitation is not in accordance with nationally recognized standards of medical practice given that further care could be provided at a lesser intensity level of care. Thus, the requested services are not medically indicated for the treatment of this patient.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 67-year-old male enrollee has requested skilled nursing care for treatment of his status post craniotomy with endoscopic removal of colloid cyst.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that skilled nursing facility services are medically necessary when there is a medical need for skilled nursing care or there is an expectation for practical improvement with skilled therapies based on realistic goals. This patient required maximum assistance for mobility and activities of daily living and demonstrated cognitive issues following surgery. As of the date in question, the patient required maximum assistance for activities of daily living, transfers and ambulation. A week later, the records indicate the patient was “unable to follow directions with the rehab team” and was maximum dependent (times two) for transfers. The patient did not progress and did not demonstrate practical change during his skilled nursing facility rehabilitation. Further, there is no documentation of a need for wound care or other nursing services as of the said date. The patient’s needs as of this date were custodial. Continued skilled nursing services were no longer medically necessary, as the patient did not demonstrate a medical need for continued skilled nursing or an expectation for improvement with skilled therapies. All told, skilled nursing care from the dates in question was not and is not medically necessary for the treatment of this patient.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient

Findings:  The physician reviewer found that this patient sustained clavicular, rib and pubic ramus fractures. As recommended by the medical literature, these injuries are typically managed non-operatively (Anderson; Denard, et al.; Hill, et al.). As of the date in question, the patient had progressed to a level of function where further care could be provided at a less intensive level of care such as home health care as planned. The patient’s records document that she has been medically stable. Further, her pain has been well controlled and her leg edema has improved. She has multiple chronic medical issues, but these issues can be followed on an outpatient basis without an expectation of a significant difference in health or functional outcomes. There are no reported skilled nursing issues in that the patient is on an oral diet and oral or inhaled medications and is not reported to require complex wound care or other skilled nursing services. From a functional standpoint, she is able to walk household distances and perform ADLs at the standby assist level. The patient’s needs as of the date in question onward were and are custodial in nature; the medical necessity of SNF services beyond this date has not been established.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 30-year-old female enrollee has requested inpatient cognitive rehabilitation for treatment of her traumatic brain injury.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that at this time, there is a lack of consensus or supporting data demonstrating that the increased intensity offered by an inpatient cognitive rehabilitation program mid-course in an individual’s recovery results in meaningful gains sustained beyond six months. Rehabilitation after brain injury, traumatic or otherwise, is very much tied to the brain's recovery. As the brain recovers rehabilitation sustains and maximizes the recovery. If the brain does not regain function, continued rehabilitation does not change the outcome. Given the patient’s injury, she will need a sustained rehabilitation program. She is independent in many of her functional activities but needs supervision and cuing. While it is reasonable and appropriate for the patient to participate in a sustained program of cognitive rehabilitation, there is no evidence to support the requested inpatient cognitive rehabilitation as medically necessary for this patient.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 22-year-old female enrollee has requested acute inpatient treatment for treatment of her behavioral health issues.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the patient’s medical records do not clearly and adequately support the primary and secondary diagnoses. The providers first deny the existence of an eating disorder, and then describe the patient’s history of an eating disorder that had persisted for about three years. In addition, she was switched from the mood disorders program to the eating disorders program ostensibly because of age of the patient population and not due to her primary disorder. She had an EEG performed with positive findings, which were not apparently further investigated. Despite this disparity, the patient was prescribed at least one medication that could enhance seizures. Applying the criteria set forth by the American Psychiatric Association (APA), this patient’s records do not substantiate the clinical necessity for the intensive, 24-hour monitoring and supervision provided during the period at issue. The patient’s history and symptoms suggest that she could have been safely and adequately treated in a less restrictive level of care such as intensive outpatient program (IOP) or outpatient care.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care

Findings:  The physician reviewer found that according to the home care notes that were submitted, the patient has no seizure activity, no oxygen requirement and no significant routine medications. She receives breathing treatments on an as-needed basis, and she requires intermittent chest physiotherapy and suctioning because she cannot handle secretions. Caregivers perform basic functions such as feeding, bathing, and changing diapers, as well as some therapeutic interventions like range of motion exercises and developmentally-appropriate stimulation.  Based on the submitted documentation, all of the care she receives is custodial and maintenance in nature. This patient’s current needs do not require the expertise of skilled nursing, and her care can be provided by trained unskilled caregivers.  All told, continued in-home skilled nursing services are not medically indicated for this patient.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The parent of a 17-year-old female enrollee has requested acute intensive psychiatric inpatient services and partial hospital program (PHP) care for treatment of the enrollee’s behavioral health issues.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that this patient’s records document that she had been treated for severe, recurrent major depression with suicidal ideation for two years prior to the onset of her eating disorder. She also has had a history of self harm with cutting. Following the above described admission, the patient cycled into a manic episode while being treated on an antidepressant. She was readmitted as an inpatient, and subsequently discharged to the partial hospitalization program(PHP) on the date in question. Her team of treating providers indicated that the patient was thought to require this level of care as she was not safe to be at a lower level of care at that point. Clearly, with a new diagnosis of bipolar disorder, accompanied by a recent diagnosis of anorexia nervosa and a co-morbid diagnosis of PTSD, an adjustment period was necessary. It is important to achieve full resolution of symptoms of the current episode in an attempt to improve the patient’s behaviors (Thomas and colleagues). Given the patient’s recent history of purging anything consumed and loss of 12 pounds within 1 month prior to admission, both psychopharmacologically and psychologically, the medical necessity has been established for her treatment at the acute inpatient level of care and follow-up therapy in the PHP through the requested dates.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of a four-month-old male enrollee has requested skilled nursing services for treatment of the enrollee’s congenital dislocation of the right knee. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that a congenital dislocation of the knee is a rare medical condition. There is a lack of support in the medical literature documenting a requirement for skilled nursing services during preoperative or postoperative care in these patients.  Based on the medical documentation provided, the services at issue were not medically indicated. During the orthopedic visits, an assessment was provided by the clinic nurse. During the time of serial casting, prior to surgery, the patient was taking ibuprofen for pain.  Postoperatively, the patient was taking Tylenol with codeine. There are no other specific nursing procedures prescribed by the physician. The submitted nursing notes document custodial care and standard cast care for this patient.  The patient did not require documentation of vital signs.  Standard cast care, both with serial casting and postoperative care, typically does not require the services of a skilled nurse.  Pain management with the medications prescribed in this patient’s case does not typically require nursing supervision.  Therefore, the care provided by the nurse would be considered custodial in nature.  All told, skilled nursing services were not medically indicated.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: A 70-year-old male enrollee has requested continuation of hospice care while receiving chemotherapy for treatment of his medical condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the literature certainly suggests that palliative chemotherapy is an option for patients who have stage IV non-small cell lung carcinoma. In this case, the records reflect that the patient desires to continue aggressive therapy and therefore palliative chemotherapy was ordered. However, since this patient wishes to continue to pursue such treatment, he is not appropriate for hospice care at this time. The patient’s decision to continue to receive chemotherapy is not consistent with acceptance of mortality and thus does not demonstrate readiness for end-of-life care. Further, given the need to continue to monitor his response to treatment with labs and imaging, the services provided by hospice care are not medically appropriate for this patient. All told, the submitted evidence demonstrates that the patient is not ready to receive end-of-life care, and therefore, hospice care is not medically necessary at this time. If the patient decides that chemotherapy is no longer desired, or that it can no longer be tolerated, hospice care would then be medically appropriate.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: A 54-year-old female enrollee has requested home infusion of lactated Ringer solution (2 liters per day) for treatment of her chronic fibromyalgia and immunoglobulin deficiency. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the medical records do not show a clear definitive diagnosis of fibromyalgia or Lyme disease in this patient. There is also no documentation of clinical hypovolemia in this patient. There are no signs of hypovolemia on examination, or any orthostatic changes in blood pressure or pulse. In addition, red blood cell mass and volume deficit readings, based on red blood cell mass studies, have not been clinically validated. All told, there is insufficient evidence that the patient meets clinical indications for lactated Ringer’s solution. In the absence of clinical practice guidelines or randomized studies demonstrating the appropriateness of lactated Ringer’s solution in this setting, the medical necessity of the requested therapy is not established.

Findings: A 43-year-old male enrollee has for continued skilled nursing facility (SNF) care level III (including pain management via IV analgesic infusion) for treatment of his medical condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that palliative care is often labor-intensive (see Zerzan and colleagues). Optimal care of an end-stage cancer patient often requires highly individualized care and continuity of care by caregivers who have an established relationship with the patient (see Hanson and colleagues). A review of the records reveals that the patient's care has been quite complex and has required close and skilled monitoring with frequent adjustments in his IV medications. The patient’s current level III SNF setting has provided the necessary and appropriate care, particularly in the area of his pain management. A transfer to an alternate level II SNF setting could compromise the pain control that has been achieved on his current PCA pump regimen, and would disrupt his continuity of care.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The representative of a 53-year-old male enrollee has requested for acute rehabilitation services for treatment of the enrollee’s medical condition, status-post cerebrovascular accident (CVA). Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the records do not outline specific and identifiable goals which would require such an acute rehabilitation environment, nor do they outline any goals which could not be addressed alternatively at a lesser level of care, including a skilled nursing facility. The lack of identifying acute rehabilitation goals is additionally supported by the patient’s past rehabilitation course, and by the patient’s ongoing dementia/delirium, which suggest that the patient would have a limited capacity for carryover in rehabilitation from one session to the next. Further, there is no medical evidence in the submitted documentation demonstrating that this patient regressed as a result of discharge to a skilled nursing facility. Additionally, the records do not document any specific care or supervision need which could not be met at a skilled nursing facility.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The representative of a 62-year-old female enrollee has requested resumption of acute inpatient rehabilitation for treatment of the enrollee, who is status post cerebrovascular accident. Findings:  The physician reviewer found the patient’s functional status had plateaued. Treatment goals had been achieved and had even been exceeded with respect to ambulation. Therefore, additional acute inpatient rehabilitation beyond the date of service in question was not clinically indicated.  In order to qualify for continued acute inpatient rehabilitation services, an individual should be continuing to demonstrate significant and measurable progress toward stated goals. Once progress has plateaued or slowed to the point where further gains will be limited and/or slow to achieve, patients are generally discharged from acute inpatient rehabilitation and transitioned to a less intensive level of rehabilitation services. In this patient’s case, resumption of acute inpatient rehabilitation is not medically indicated.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 49-year-old male enrollee has requested rehabilitation at a skilled nursing facility for the treatment of his medical condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the medical literature indicates that recovery after stroke occurs fastest in the first three months. Later recovery (up to one to two years after stroke) is also possible, especially between three to six months. Therefore, continued rehabilitation is generally appropriate for a patient who has had a recent stroke (within the last three months). While this patient’s condition was somewhat limited by his medical problems, he demonstrated some improvement during his stay in the skilled nursing facility and was continuing to progress.  In light of his capacity for further improvement, his continued stay during the time period in question was medically appropriate and indicated. Further, it is reasonable to provide the patient with additional skilled nursing facility services at this time. While the patient’s progress has been slow, there continues to be potential for improvement. Moreover, a skilled nursing setting will allow the patient’s medical problems to be addressed thus maximizing the amount of therapy that he can tolerate.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 45-year-old female enrollee has requested additional physical therapy at a skilled care facility for treatment of her medical condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that there is general agreement that skilled rehabilitation is appropriate for individuals with a hip fracture. However, there is no consensus on the effectiveness of different therapeutic programs (i.e., in terms of intensity, duration, and frequency). The need for continued skilled rehabilitation depends on the individual’s response to therapy and whether further gains are likely. This patient’s weight bearing status was toe-touch weight bearing. The patient required minimal assistance with her bed mobility, transfers, and walking. She required moderate assistance in most activities of daily living. The patient was independent in bed mobility and transfers on and required stand-by-assistance with walking (using a front-wheeled walker). The records indicate the patient either required stand-by-assistance or was independent in her activities of daily living. Per the physical therapy note, the patient had met her goals by ambulating greater than 100 feet with stand-by-assistance with her walker and was independent with her bed mobility and transfers. She had also met her occupational therapy goals. The patient was trained in safety and exercises and instructed on how to follow her weight bearing precautions. The physical therapy notes conclude by stating that the patient was ready to be discharged. All told, the patient made significant progress in her rehabilitation program. Although she required stand-by-assistance with ambulation, and likely still requires this level of assistance with ambulation, it is not necessary for this assistance to be provided by skilled therapists. The submitted evidence does not demonstrate that the patient has functional deficits that require additional skilled physical therapy at this time.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 58-year-old male enrollee has requested continued skilled nursing inpatient stay for acute physical therapy for treatment of his quadriplegia secondary to spinal cord injury. Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 62-year-old male enrollee has requested post-acute inpatient rehabilitation services for treatment of his medical condition status post intracranial hemorrhage.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) guidelines suggest that patients may be appropriate candidates for continued inpatient rehabilitation when they are reasonably expected to make measurable and practical functional gains within a reasonable period of time. It is also assumed that these patients would not progress at a similar rate in a less intensive rehabilitation setting. This patient's progress appears to haved slowed considerably and it is likely that any future gains achieved in a post-acute inpatient rehabilitation program would be similar to those obtained in a less intensive setting. Approximately three months post intracranial hemorrhage, the records provided for review indicate that he had begun to plateau from a functional perspective. While the patient may continue to demonstrate recovery of function over time, it is likely that the recovery curve will be gradual. In light of this, as well as the paucity of randomized clinical trials demonstrating therapeutic benefit of the requested services in this setting , inpatient rehabilitation services are not likely to result in greater or more rapid functional improvement than a less intensive level of care.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The representative of a 60-year-old male enrollee has requested skilled nursing care for treatment of the enrollee, who is status post cerebrovascular accident. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the patient continued with right hemiplegia and was not making significant progress with physical therapy and occupational therapy. Per his attending physician, he was alert and appropriate, but demonstrated mild confusion at times. His other medical conditions were stable, and he was not requiring a minimum of two hours of daily nursing by a registered nurse. Per the reference by Goroll and Mulley, the patient was receiving appropriate care post cerebrovascular accident. He was admitted to a rehabilitation facility and received skilled level of care therapies. His cerebrovascular accident was completed, and he was receiving secondary prevention with blood pressure control, control of dyslipidemia with fish oil and niacin, and treatment with Plavix. His diabetic control was adequate, as the patient has an insulin pump. Rehabilitation post cerebrovascular accident should involve assessment, goal setting, interventions and reassessment. The potential for success is enhanced by a multidisciplinary approach in a structured setting. The submitted documentation indicates the patient had reached maximum benefit from skilled rehabilitation level of care as of the last authorized date of service. Per the patient’s attending physician, plans were in progress for disposition to a lower level of care. The patient was tolerating an oral diet and had no wound care needs requiring skilled nursing level of care. Additionally, the patient had plateaued in skilled therapies.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 61-year-old female enrollee has requested skilled rehabilitation for the treatment of her medical condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the medical records demonstrates that while in the skilled nursing facility the patient was alert and oriented, continent, had a foley catheter, medically stable, and did not require parenteral medications or skin care. She was receiving bladder training and daily physical therapy. Initially she was non-ambulatory due to her non-weight bearing status, but was eventually cleared for toe-touch weight bearing status and was able to ambulate with a front-wheeled-walker with moderate assistance. Her transfer status was stand-by-assistance. Her ambulatory status eventually progressed to contact-guard assistance and her bed mobility increased to an independent level. However, her weight bearing status was changed back to non-weight bearing due to concern about the healing of her fracture. The patient received occupational therapy and she gained steady progress in that area with most of her difficulty being in donning her socks. All told, this patient required skilled rehabilitation and was making progress with her mobility training, activities of daily living training, and bladder training throughout this period. However, due to her weight-bearing status being changed back to non-weight bearing, further significant progress was not expected with her activities of daily living or her mobility training. In addition, her bladder training had ceased. In summary, the patient had achieved her maximum potential with her activities of daily living and mobility given her new weight-bearing status with further significant progress not being expected.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The parent and conservator of a 40-year-old female enrollee has requested transfer to an out-of-network facility for brain rehabilitation following the enrollee’s traumatic brain injury. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that there is no evidence that intensive neurological rehabilitation has a role in the care of patients who are unresponsive. The intensity and effective duration of such therapy is debated even for patients less seriously injured. The medical care for patients with severe head injury is a serious and complex matter. The Health Plan’s recommendations for consultation are appropriate and helpful, but most of the patient’s needs are custodial in nature, as there is no evidence or expectation that a comprehensive neuro-rehabilitation program will benefit an unresponsive person. There is no defined medical therapy that can be expected to improve outcome although anecdotal reports abound. Unfortunately, these reports do not provide a guide to a coherent systematic approach that can be expected to provide any benefit. At any rate, medical or pharmacological interventions designed to improve cognitive function can be employed at the patient’s current residence, especially in consultation with specialists as the Health Plan has suggested. There is no medical necessity for a move to a comprehensive center.  Finally, examination of her limbs found she was receiving satisfactory care with splinting, medication, and passive range of motion exercises for joint mobility.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The wife of a now deceased male enrollee has requested an extension of the skilled nursing facility (SNF) stay for physical and occupational therapy services for the treatment of the enrollee’s acute renal failure and multiple myeloma. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the patient was functionally impaired on admission to the SNF. The skilled care he needed was to restore function. Skilled rehabilitation services are appropriate for patients with the functional capacity to participate and benefit from the services. Dialysis patients certainly can benefit as this patient demonstrated. Functional capacity, not diagnosis, determines benefit. Clearly, the patient progressed in a clinically appropriate and expected manner.  The services were ordered appropriately and provided appropriately. The skilled rehabilitation services were best provided on an inpatient basis.

Hence, in this setting there can be no significant improvement expected with continued daily skilled PT/OT in a reasonable period of time. Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 78-year-old male enrollee has requested skilled nursing facility (SNF) services for the treatment of his multiple injuries. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the patient’s condition does not respond to therapeutic pharmaceuticals. Brain healing determines progress. The submitted documentation reveals that continued PT showed a decline from the peak. The patient was progressing with OT, but the rate and area of progression indicate limited capacity to regain function. As discussed in the paper by Gordon et al., the progress for recovery following traumatic brain injury can continue for extended periods of time, but the extent of brain injury and the rate of brain injury determine the rate of functional recovery. Continued PT and OT cannot hasten functional recovery in the absence of brain recovery, nor do they promote brain recovery. Because the patient was progressing and did progress, the Health Plan’s denial should be overturned for the first round of therapy and upheld for the second round.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 46-year-old male enrollee has requested continued rehabilitation therapies and skilled nursing services for the treatment of the enrollee, who is status post pelvic fracture. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the patient was not safe for discharge during the dates of service at issue, and he was progressing with physical therapy and occupational therapy. His needs were not custodial. The prevailing practice standard is to complete rehabilitation for patients transferred to a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation. In this case, the patient’s skilled nursing facility-based rehabilitation was not complete as of the last authorized date of service and it would not have been reasonable to provide the patient with a lower level of care. The Health Plan’s assessment of the patient’s needs was not consistent with his clinical course in rehabilitation.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The representative of a 56-year-old male enrollee has requested for continued care at a skilled nursing facility (SNF) for treatment of his cerebral vascular accident (CVA).    Findings:  The physician reviewer found that there is no expectation that continued daily skilled rehabilitation services will significantly alter the patient’s functional status. The literature is very clear – skilled rehabilitation does not increase neurological recovery. Additionally, the level of function the patient has reached places him at a level that no longer requires inpatient services. His needs for assistance could be met at a lower level of care.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 63-year-old female enrollee has requested continued skilled nursing facility services for the treatment of her condition. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that daily skilled PT and OT are not medically necessary when progress does not continue. Such intense services are not necessary to maintain functional gains. The intense skilled services are necessary to monitor and instruct a patient who is recovering from functional loss.  However, once the recovery has occurred or once a stable functional level has been attained, gains can be maintained with a stable exercise routine that does not require daily PT or OT oversight.  I concur with the denial as the requested services are not necessary, and are not reasonably expected to benefit the enrollee.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
