Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The representative of a 65-year-old male enrollee has requested continued rehabilitation services (physical and occupational therapy) at a skilled nursing facility for the treatment of the enrollee, who is status post CVA. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that the rationale for the denial appears to be related to social resources. The patient was denied continued rehabilitation because he would remain in a skilled nursing facility and require 24 hour supervision. The rationale is independent of the clinical progress he was making, albeit slowly. On 5/29/08, the patient required moderate assistance with bed mobility and moderate/minimal assistance with transfers. Two weeks prior, he was moderate/maximum to maximum assist in these modalities. He showed similar progress with occupational therapy. His progress precludes predicting what his precise functional gain will be. There are no clinical algorithms or other predictive tables that permit such a prediction. He is unlikely to gain neurologic recovery, and his progress with rehabilitation is slow, but the standard for stopping rehabilitation is that the patient has reached a functional plateau and is not expected to benefit from additional intensive rehabilitation, as opposed to range of motion or exercise.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The parent of a three-year-old male enrollee has requested authorization and coverage for at-home applied behavioral analysis (ABA) therapy for treatment of the enrollee’s autism.  Findings:  The physician reviewer found that although review of the literature reveals no citations evaluating the differences between in-home ABA and clinically based ABA, most ABA programs provided today have at least some component of in-home treatment. The ultimate goal of any ABA program is to have the patient functioning independently in the community.  Independent functioning must begin in the home with self-help skills and family communications.  All the social/play and perspective taking skills as well as the self-help skills (especially continence) should take place in the home. The patient will have a need for future self-help skill goals as he becomes developmentally age-appropriate. It is often difficult to have these skills carry over into the home if taught in an outside environment. All behavioral programs should involve training of the parents/caregivers to allow for carry-over from the behavioral sessions.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The patient is a five-year-old male with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS). He underwent surgery in October 2005 for placement of diaphragmatic pacemakers. Previously, he had a tracheostomy and required mechanical ventilation. The patient was successfully decannulated in July 2006, and has since been monitored at night with continuous pulse oximetry and home health nursing. Nursing notes have documented normal oxygen saturations at night with no need for supplemental oxygen. However, multiple nurses have described very restless sleep and the need for frequent repositioning to maintain the integrity of the pacers and to ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation. The parent’s request for continued authorization of home health nursing services (84 hours per week) was denied by the Health Plan based upon a determination that these services are no longer medically necessaryCCHS is an extremely rare disorder characterized by “generally adequate ventilation while the patient is awake but alveolar hypoventilation with typically normal respiratory rates and shallow breathing (diminished tidal volume) during sleep.” Those who are more severely affected demonstrate hypoventilation during wakefulness as well as sleep. All CCHS patients lack the appropriate arousal response to hypoxemia and hypercarbia, putting them at long-term risk for cardiac abnormalities (e.g. right heart failure), pulmonary hypertension, and death. Generally, the management of CCHS involves ventilatory support: tracheostomy with mechanical ventilation or diaphragmatic pacing. Diaphragmatic pacing may allow more freedom for those who require ventilatory support only during sleep. Children with CCHS must be managed with extreme vigilance. There is no inherent physiological response to hypoxemia or hypercarbia. Even during waking hours, these children will not experience shortness of breath in response to pneumonia or increase their respiratory rate in response to physical exertion. Frequently, patients with CCHS will not develop fever in response to infection. Severe respiratory distress can occur with minimal external manifestations. In addition, children with CCHS do not pace themselves appropriately during strenuous exercise because they cannot sense hypoxemia or hypercarbia. The literature also reports that “autonomic dysfunction and cardiac abnormalities are common in CCHS.”The patient is at significant risk for complications from his disorder. He is being successfully managed now with vigilant nursing care while he sleeps. Not only does the home health nursing staff ensure adequate functioning of the pacers, but their constant vigilance allows for early identification and intervention with any event that could compromise the patient’s already tenuous cardiopulmonary status. Therefore, I have determined the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 50-year-old male who was hospitalized with intracranial hemorrhage and leukemia. He had dramatically impaired consciousness. The patient was receiving IV antibiotics and PE tube feedings. An intracranial shunt was placed. He remained at an acute inpatient level of care through August 2006. The Health Plan indicates the patient could have been transferred to a sub acute level of care as of July 2006.Review of the submitted clinical evidence indicates the patient was stabilized by July 2006 and off antibiotics by July 2006. As of July 2006, the treatment plan was to discharge the patient to a skilled nursing facility. There was no change in the patient’s condition in July 2006 warranting continuation at an acute level of care. He was transferred to a recovery floor and was no longer in an acute medical unit. All of the patient’s medical issues were chronic in nature as of the last authorized date of service. All acute conditions had been addressed and stabilized by July 2006 and therefore there was no indication for continued acute hospitalization.For the reasons stated above, I have determined the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 24-year-old male with a three-year history of polysubstance abuse including cocaine, alcohol and marijuana who was admitted to inpatient treatment in May 2006 following a relapse. He was involved in outpatient treatment for substance abuse for approximately five months prior to inpatient admission, and had not used any substances from November until mid March when he and some friends used alcohol and cocaine at a party. In May 2006 the patient again used alcohol and was expelled from the outpatient program. On the recommendation of his outpatient provider, he was referred for inpatient treatment. His initial diagnoses included major depression, moderate, recurrent, personality disorder, and alcohol dependence.During his inpatient course of treatment, the patient was described as motivated for treatment, cooperative and an active participant in the various therapies and 12-step meetings. He presented as euthymic with congruent affect, linear thought processes, good insight and judgment and unimpaired perceptual and thought content. He was also noted to be able to contract for safety.  The patient continued treatment with Lamictal 250mg and Celexa 40mg without adjustment of his previous outpatient dosages; his Zyprexa was discontinued.  He was not described as significantly depressed or suicidal at any point during his inpatient stay.The patient’s request for reimbursement for acute inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation services provided from May 2006 through May 2006 was denied by the Health Plan citing a lack of medical necessity. The basis for the patient’s inpatient referral is not clear; relapses often occur in this setting and do not equate to a need for inpatient treatment. The patient did not require detoxification as his use of alcohol and cocaine was highly variable, he was a willing participant in his treatment, and his depression was quiescent. It is obviously within the purview of his former outpatient program to suspend him for noncompliance with their rules, but an alternative outpatient program should have been identified prior to May 2006. All told, I have determined the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 38-year-old female with a history of alcohol abuse who was referred for residential treatment. Her home life was described as “very difficult” and she had reportedly failed numerous outpatient attempts at sobriety. The patient’s admission diagnoses were alcohol dependence and major depression and her current stressors included her marriage and remodeling of her house which necessitated temporary living arrangements. The patient had been drinking a bottle of wine per night, last doing so in April 2006; there were no reported symptoms of withdrawal. During treatment, the patient participated in therapy and was treated with Klonopin, 1mg decreased to 0.5mg, and Trazodone, up to 75mg per day. The patient was described as anxious, but there are no documented symptoms of anxiety or depression. The patient was discharged from residential treatment in May 2006. Her request for reimbursement was denied by the Health Plan based upon a determination that residential treatment services were not medically necessary.The submitted record does not indicate a severity of illness, either from an alcohol or a depressive standpoint, which would have necessitated residential treatment. The patient was apparently able to stop drinking on her own nine days prior to her residential treatment admission and there is no record that outpatient treatment was attempted as a first line approach. Additionally, despite the stated failure of numerous outpatient programs, there is no information as to the sort of programs the patient had participated in or the reasons for their failure. All told, there appears to be no clinical indications for residential treatment. Therefore, I have determined the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 62-year-old male who had a middle cerebral artery stroke in April 2006 followed by an occipital-parietal hemorrhage in April 2006. He transferred to the acute rehabilitation setting in April 2006. The level of rehabilitation progress achieved with physical therapy is unclear, but apparently was minimal as he required maximal assistance upon admission to the skilled nursing facility (SNF) in May 2006 with a dense right hemiparesis and significant deficits. PT, OT and ST report progress while he was receiving services at the SNF, but the level of progress with PT is not clearly documented. On the other hand there was clear progress with OT and ST, although quite modest as would be expected. With OT he had improvement in lower body dressing and in grooming progressing from a requirement of moderate assistance to a requirement of minimal/moderate or minimal assistance. ST reports the patient was initially unable to generate any distinct sounds, but was able to produce consonant and vowel sounds in combination and respond appropriately, though nonverbally, to inquiries with the benefit of therapy.The patient has requested authorization for skilled nursing facility services including OT, PT and ST. The Health Plan denied the request based upon a determination that the services are not medically necessary.The patient had a severe stroke resulting in severe deficits. The degree of functional recovery is likely to be modest and the rate of recovery will be slow. However, he was progressing with OT and ST and there is some evidence he was progressing with PT, but the specifics are not entirely clear. It does not appear from the records that the patient had yet achieved his maximal functional recovery, and the preponderance of evidence showed that he was progressing modestly. Rehabilitation services should be resumed and continue for as long as there is demonstrated functional gain.Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: This patient is a 47-year-old male with a history of methamphetamine abuse, depression and suicide attempts. He is hepatitis C, and HIV positive. The patient had a nine-month span of sobriety in 1999 and was again sober from June 2005 through February 2006. The patient was hospitalized for three weeks for detoxification and depression from May 2006 through June 2006. He had used intravenous (IV) methamphetamine three to four times per week before that admission. The patient was admitted to the residential care facility on the day following his hospital discharge. The record indicates he had refused sober living placement and outpatient treatment and had threatened to harm himself if not treated at a residential center. He was reportedly homeless at the time of his admission.The patient has requested reimbursement for the residential treatment services provided from June 2006 through July 2006.  The Health Plan denied the request based upon a determination that these services were not medically necessary.The documentation submitted does not demonstrate that the patient required residential treatment. Although he did have a long-standing history of methamphetamine abuse, he had been successfully detoxified prior to this admission and did not demonstrate physical symptoms of withdrawal. The patient had threatened to harm himself if he was not admitted to a residential treatment facility, however this type of manipulation does not indicate the patient was actively suicidal. There were no symptoms of homicidal ideation or active psychosis and he was medically stable at the time of admission. The patient did not require 24-hour residential care and could have continued his recovery through a partial hospitalization or intensive outpatient program. Therefore, I have determined that the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Insurer’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The patient is an 18-year-old female with cerebral palsy with spastic quadriplegia.  She is dependent for all activities of daily living. She takes nothing by mouth and uses a gastrostomy tube for all nutrition. She receives bolus feeds and is tolerating all feedings.  Her weight is stable.  She has a history of constipation, but it is manageable with medications. The patient has had no recent medical issues requiring admission to the hospital. She receives oral medications for spasticity and GI issues, but no IV medications. At issue is whether continued in-home skilled nursing care is medically necessary.Upon review of the submitted clinical records and the needs associated with this patient’s medical care there are no services that cannot be provided by a trained attendant. There is no clinical indication for skilled nursing or skilled rehabilitation services in this particular setting. The patient’s needs are custodial in nature and therefore continued in-home skilled nursing services are not warranted. Accordingly, I have determined the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 37-year-old female who was non-weight bearing after a motorcycle accident in June 2006. She received rehabilitation therapy which included sliding board transfers and activity of daily living (ADL) training. The patient progressed steadily with physical therapy (PT) from initially requiring maximum assistance in bed mobility and transfers to stand-by assistance/supervision in bed mobility and transfers and independence in wheelchair propulsion. As of July 2006 the patient required minimal to moderate assistance in toileting. In July 2006, after OT and PT were curtailed, the patient required maximal assistance for sliding board transfers. The patient has requested authorization for skilled nursing facility services provided after July 2006. The Health Plan denied her request based upon a determination that the requested services are not medically necessary.The patient was not ready for discharge in July 2006 as she was not independent in her PT and OT modalities and was continuing to make progress. Rehabilitation services continued to be medically appropriate. Additionally, the patient’s functional abilities regressed when her therapies were reduced and/or discontinued. The record indicates the patient attained weight bearing status in July 2006. SNF services should continue for one additional week and then the patient’s need for continued services should be reassessed.Based on the information cited above, I have determined the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be partially overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 63-year-old female with multiple medical problems including bipolar disorder and severe osteoarthritis. She was hospitalized in April 2006 for urosepsis complicated by acute renal failure and lithium toxicity. The patient was encephalopathic and had peripheral neuropathies during her acute stay. Her cognitive functioning improved but she had slow recovery of motor function. The patient was admitted to the skilled nursing facility (SNF) for rehabilitation in May 2006. She made good progress initially, but her progress slowed over the final two to three weeks of occupational therapy (OT) and physical therapy (PT).  Her therapists noted her osteoarthritis as contributing to her limited progress.  PT and OT services were discontinued in June 2006.  The patient and her representative have requested authorization and coverage for continued skilled nursing services.  The Health Plan denied the request citing a lack of medical necessity after June 2006.Review of the submitted clinical evidence demonstrates the patient had met her OT goals related to ADLS by week ending June 2006. She did show some increase in strength, but her functional progress was noted to be limited by her knee pain. The PT progress notes indicate limited progress in bed mobility, transfers and ambulation after week four.  It is also noted that weight bearing and ambulation were limited by her osteoarthritis. It appears that by June 2006 the patient had maximized her functional status and would not benefit further from continued inpatient skilled rehabilitation. Therefore, I have determined that continued skilled nursing facility services after June 2006 were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The patient is a 53-year-old female with right lower extremity weakness and numbness. The patient reports that she requires help from her husband to get to her medical appointments. Prior to her illness she was independent in her daily living activities, and had complete mobility with shopping, driving, etc. A home physical therapy evaluation was performed in June 2006. The patient has requested authorization and coverage for home health physical therapy, which has been denied by the Health Plan on the basis that it is not medically necessary.The submitted documentation indicates the patient has gait disturbance. She had an evaluation for physical therapy in her home in June 2006. She was noted to be independent with mobility but had impaired balance, impaired right lower extremity sensation, decreased right lower extremity (1-3 of 5), and was also noted to walk with a front-wheeled walker. Based upon the evidence provided, the patient requires home physical therapy as she remains homebound at this time. She is unable to leave her home without assistance from another person. She has experienced a decline in her level of function as a result of illness and therefore requires physical therapy to improve her right lower extremity strength and balance and regain her prior level of ambulation without requiring assistance. Therefore, I have determined the requested therapy is medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 74-year-old male who was admitted to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) for rehabilitation and wound care after an acute hospital stay for congestive heart failure and COPD. In May 2006, his wound was documented as 1.1cm by 1.0cm in size and the wound care involved cleansing with normal saline and the application of a dry dressing and foam padding. The patient was functionally impaired, requiring caregiver assistance or stand-by assistance with bed mobility, transfers and ambulation. The patient has requested authorization for continued care at the SNF.  The Health Plan denied the request based upon a determination that continued SNF services are not medically necessary.By the end of May 2006, the patient had improved significantly.  He had progressed to the point that he was independent or “moderately independent” with bed mobility, transfers, ambulation and navigation of stairs (two) and was able to ambulate 250’ with a front wheel walker.  His wound was described as 0.4cm by 0.5cm in size with a red wound bed and surrounding skin areas in May 2006.  The Panafil ointment for debridement was discontinued in May 2006. There is no depth measurement or wound staging documented and no wound assessment after May 2006.  The patient was taking oral nutrition and was described as having an increased energy level.  His wound was small and the relatively simple wound care could have been performed at home if continued care was needed.  The patient was appropriate for discharge home by the end of May 2006.Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The patient is a 46-year-old male with muscular dystrophy and respiratory failure after an episode of pneumonia. He is now on ventilation and can be off the ventilator for a few hours per day. He is tolerating a portable (home) ventilator. Family members have demonstrated the ability to suction and bag with the ventilator. The patient’s family has requested authorization for home health care services. The Health Plan has determined that discharge to home is not medically appropriate or safe and therefore has recommended placement in a sub-acute facility. There is no data in the records indicating the patient cannot be adequately cared for in an in-home setting. Sub-acute care is not inherently safer or superior to at-home care, especially if the family is appropriately trained. The submitted evidence demonstrates the patient’s family has received caregiver training and the patient is able to tolerate home ventilation. He is receiving tube feedings. The evidence provided does not identify specific safety concerns necessitating sub-acute care. As such, home health cares services are medically appropriate and should be authorized by the Health Plan. Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is an 85-year-old female with a history of mitral valve repair and embolic shower. This resulted in necrosis of the fingers on her right hand, and a below the knee amputation on the right and a metatarsal amputation on the left. She also has residual eschar. Her wounds are stable and require daily dressing (application of ointment). There is no evidence the patient’s wounds are green or draining or require packing. She undergoes a daily dressing change only. The wound on the patient’s buttocks does not exceed stage II and requires no more than a duoderm dressing. A request has been made for coverage for the patient’s continued stay at a skilled nursing facility after April 2006.  The Health Plan has denied the request on the basis the services are not medically necessary.Review of the submitted clinical evidence demonstrates the patient’s wounds were stable after April 2006. Her wounds can be appropriately addressed in a variety of settings: home, assisted living, or outpatient. The patient’s wound care and overall medical condition do not require daily inpatient care because her wounds are stable and only require application of medicinal ointment and clean dressing. There are no medical issues of high complexity involved in this case. Therefore, I have determined that continued skilled nursing facility services after April 2006 were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 53-year old male admitted for acute medical care in November 2005 continuing through March 2006.  He underwent LVAD placement in December 2005 and closure of tongue wounds in March 2006.  He had a subsequent rupture of the tongue wound with massive bleeding and returned to surgery.  The patient participated in physical and occupational therapy during his acute medical hospitalization.  According to the physical therapy notes he received physical therapy twice per day in March 2006 with LVAD precautions. He required moderate two person assistance to stand and transfer and minimal assistance for ambulation from 120 to 600 feet. As of March 2006 he was independent with upper body activities of daily living (ADLs) and needed maximal assistance with lower body ADLs.  The patient was transferred to the acute rehabilitation program in March 2006 and was not taking anything by mouth at that time.  He was fed via nasogastric tube secondary to his tongue wound. He worked closely with speech therapy and began oral feeding in March 2006.  The patient required careful monitoring to advance his diet.  Per the physician notes, at the time of admission the patient had an LVAD, a PICC line, several open wounds, and required careful medical monitoring by his physician.  Physical and occupational therapy findings during acute rehabilitation were consistent with his previous therapy. He continued to make slow progress through March 2006 when he was discharged home.The patient’s request for reimbursement for the acute rehabilitation services was denied by the Health Plan based upon a determination that the services were not medically necessary.Based on the records provided, the patient’s primary rehabilitation issue was general deconditioning.  In most cases this problem in and of itself, would not have required acute rehabilitation and the patient’s progress with therapy was somewhat slow. However, the patient’s medical problems were significant and he required daily medical evaluation and acute nursing care in addition to his on-going rehabilitation needs. The necessary level of medical care could not have been provided in a subacute or skilled rehabilitation program. Therefore, I have determined the services at issue were medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is an 82-year-old female who sustained a right hip fracture in February 2004 and a left hip fracture in April 2004. The patient was admitted to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in May 2004. She began physical and occupational therapy in that same month. She progressed steadily with therapy. Physical and occupational therapy were discontinued in June 2004. The patient was discharged from the SNF later that same month. At issue is whether continued skilled nursing facility services were medically necessary as of June 2004.  Based on the records provided, the patient had not reached a plateau as of June 2004. She could not safely be discharged to home as of that date. The clinical evidence demonstrates that as of June 2004 the patient was progressing with therapy and there was an expectation she would continue to progress with additional therapy. The patient did not reach a plateau or near plateau until mid-June 2004. As such, the SNF services the patient received were medically appropriate and indicated through mid-June 2004.Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined the services at issue were medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition through mid-June 2004. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial should be partially overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 38-year-old male who sustained a fall in July 2005 with resultant bilateral calcaneal/lumbar fracture. He was hospitalized then transferred to skilled nursing care in August 2005. Once there, he received extensive physical and occupational therapy. The patient was ultimately discharged in December 2005. The Health Plan denied coverage for skilled nursing facility services as of October 2005 on the basis that continued services were not medically necessary.Review of the submitted medical documentation indicates the patient no longer required a level of skilled care services as of October 2005. He was stable for outpatient physical therapy at that time. He no longer required wound care after September 2005. The physical therapy notes state the patient completed his initial goals as of September 2005 and was re-evaluated on October 2005 with new goals established including improved transfer, increased balance and increased gait capacity. A physical therapy notation from October 2005 indicates the patient had made significant progress in all balance and functional mobility activities. He was described as “independent of gait throughout and continued to fatigue quickly with steps.” The patient was medically stable and able to perform all transfers, toileting and showers independently. As such, continued skilled nursing facility services were not medically necessary or indicated as of October 2005. Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: A 39-year-old female enrollee requested authorization and coverage of daily home health services. The Health Plan  denied the request indicating that the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the enrollee’s infected surgical incision status post cesarean section.One physician reviewer performed a medical necessity Independent Medical Review. The physician reviewer upheld the Health Plan’s denial on the basis that the requested services are not medically necessary.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 45-year-old male with a history of anemia, hepatic encephalopathy and cirrhosis. He was admitted to acute care in October 2005 with acute alcohol intoxication. He was admitted to a skilled care facility (SNF) in October 2005. A physical therapy evaluation performed in October 2005 found the patient was alert and able to ambulate independently. The patient’s provider switched the patient from intravenous antibiotics to oral antibiotics and recommended discontinuation of skilled therapy. The Health Plan denied coverage for continued SNF services as of October 2005. At issue is whether continued SNF services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition.Based upon the evidence provided, the patient does not meet medical necessity criteria for continued SNF services. The submitted records indicate the patient was alert and oriented in October 2005 and was independent with mobility and ambulation. The patient does not require physical or occupational therapy and has no need for daily skilled nursing services. Though it appears the patient would benefit from treatment of his alcohol dependence, there is no indication for continued SNF services. Therefore, I have determined the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 60-year-old male who has a history of severe pulmonary hypertension, diabetes mellitus, morbid obesity, and displaced left trimalleolar fractures. He was placed in a skilled nursing facility and occupational therapy and physical therapy were initiated. It appears occupational therapy was discontinued in September 2005. The Health Plan denied authorization and coverage for SNF services as of September 2005. At issue is whether continued SNF services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s condition.The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld. The submitted evidence indicates the patient reached a stable level with activities of daily living as of September 2005. In addition, the patient was at a stable level with physical therapy with standby assistance. Therapy notes from September 2005 indicate the patient could climb four steps with use of a quad cane. Based upon the documentation provided, the patient’s status as of September 2005 was such that he no longer required a SNF level of care and was appropriate for discharge. Therefore, I have determined the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 61-year-old female who sustained a fractured right femur and is status post open reduction and internal fixation. She also has a complex medical history, which includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, hypothyroidism and schizophrenia. She needed maximum assistance with bathing and dressing. She also required assistance with transfers and ambulation, as she was unable to ambulate by herself. She made no progress during her stay in August 2005 so occupational therapy was discontinued. The patient is seeking coverage for further SNF services.The patient is clinically stable. The patient has no on-going daily skilled nursing needs and there is no documented progress with physical therapy or occupational therapy. In addition, there is no evidence that currently the patient is able to benefit from physical or occupational therapy. Because the patient is clinically stable, has no daily skilled needs, and is not benefiting for rehabilitation therapy, I have determined the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 63-year-old male with lower back pain secondary to osteomyelitis who was admitted to a skilled nursing facility after a hospital admission.  The patient had a physical therapy evaluation in April 2005. At that time the patient required minimum assistance for bed mobility, moderate assistance with transfers, and minimum assistance with ambulation. In addition, the patient required minimum assistance with toilet hygiene and maximum assistance with lower back dressing and bathing. After seven days of therapy, the patient required contact guard assistance with bed mobility, contact guard assistance with transfers, and contact guard assistance with ambulation. At this time the patient had not completed his rehabilitation course and was expected to continue to progress. He had not reached his functional potential and he was not independent or safe to be alone. The patient continued to receive therapy until May 2005. The Health Plan has denied reimbursement for the services the patient received after 5/5/05.The patient was denied continued rehabilitation therapy after seven sessions of physical and occupational therapy without achieving safe independent function. The patient’s coverage was denied before he completed his rehabilitation course. The clinical evidence demonstrates the patient was progressing with therapy and that there was an expectation he would continue to progress towards independence with continued therapy. The skilled therapy the patient received until 5/18/05 was medically necessary and appropriate. There is no indication this patient was at a custodial level of care during the dates of service in question.Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined the services at issue were medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 64-year-old male with hepatitis encephalopathy resulting in a seven-day hospital admission. The patient had an onset of his condition approximately two to three days prior to hospitalization. During the hospitalization records indicate the patient experienced deconditioning. Records further indicate the patient’s spouse was not able to care for the patient. After hospitalization the patient began receiving skilled therapy. The Health Plan provided coverage for the skilled nursing facility (SNF) services the patient received until 3/25/05 – at which time the Health Plan determined further SNF services were not medically necessary. The patient is requesting coverage for continued SNF services.The patient received physical and occupational therapy from 3/16/05 to 3/25/05. During this time period the patient’s cognitive status had improved. On 3/22/05, he was minimum assist for transfers and minimum assist for ambulation. Although he could ambulate 30 feet, having progressed from 10 feet, his only progress was in distance. At the time of the Health Plan’s denial the patient was not independent and required at least minimum assistance for his activities of daily living and transfers. Furthermore, there is no evidence the patient could have been safely discharged home at the time of the Health Plan’s denial. Although the patient’s rehabilitation capacity may be limited, the extent of his ability to recover was not established. A 10-day course of rehabilitation therapy is not expected to be sufficient given the patient’s hospital length of stay and his pre-morbid status. The records reveal the patient remained a candidate for SNF services as of 3/25/05 as there is no evidence the patient had reached his maximum level of function and there is evidence that he would continue to progress with continued therapy.Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial should be overturned. Based upon the information provided the patient should be evaluated on 4/14/05 to determine whether continued SNF services are necessary or whether the patient can be safely and effectively discharged from skilled care.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 35-year-old female with an approximate eight-year history of alcohol dependence, consisting of drinking a bottle of wine per night and apparently significantly more on the weekends. This resulted in verbally abusive (and what had been deemed “manic”) behavior. Her boyfriend who lives with her had noted dreading the weekends due to the extent of her drinking and subsequent unruliness. The patient also has a past history of anorexia and bulimia, though she reported this as in good control with Zoloft 200mg. She has not been formally diagnosed with bipolar disorder despite the history of becoming manic when drinking.The patient initially entered residential treatment on 12/30/04 with the request to learn how to cut down on her drinking, but still be able to drink socially. However, she was receptive to being told that this was a frequent folly of alcohol dependent individuals, noted by the clinician as “she accepted this option without further question or argument.” The patient did not have a history of withdrawal symptoms and none are documented in the information provided. Treatment notes from 1/2/05 indicate the patient was “very congenial and friendly, seems open-minded to treatment. Maybe ambivalence, not sure.” On 1/3/05, she was noted as “more comfortable with residents and peers. Client utilized group process more willingly and openly today by sharing self and feelings.” On 1/7/05, it was noted the patient was “distraught, wanting to leave program and ‘go ahead and relapse’ since hearing that insurance will not support her level of care.” However, by 1/9/05, she was noted as “cheerful and bouyant all morning” as well as “grateful for her sobriety.” The submitted notes indicate the patient did sneak alcohol into residential care on two occasions, though she drank a lesser amount at those times.The patient has requested coverage for residential treatment services from 1/6/05 onward. The Health Plan has denied the patient’s request indicating the patient could have been treated at a less intensive level of care as of 1/6/05.All told, there appears little evidence in the submitted documentation to indicate the patient was not appropriate for transfer to a less intensive level of care by 1/6/05. Though the fact that the patient snuck alcohol into residential treatment on two occasions does indicate the patient’s ambivalence about sobriety, this no more argues for the need for residential treatment that it does for intensive outpatient treatment. If anything, if a patient is really that intent on drinking, neither residential treatment nor intensive outpatient treatment is likely to be successful. As such, residential treatment services were no longer medically indicated as of 1/6/05. Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined that the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 59-year-old female with a long-standing history of alcohol dependence and depression, drinking approximately two bottles of wine and four vodka mixed drinks each night for the past two and a half years, to the point of blacking out every night for the three months prior to admission to residential treatment on 7/27/04. The patient related the increased drinking to an increasing level of depression, which was related to a series of losses. These included her mother’s decline and death from Alzheimer’s disease, loss of some friends, an extremely stressful job, and living by herself. She was previously treated on an outpatient basis with Paxil 20mg with little perceived benefit. Pertinent social history otherwise included her emanating from a family in which her father was strongly alcohol dependent, and the patient having been married and divorced three times, with no children, and no longer involved in any intimate relationship. Upon admission to residential treatment, she was noted as depressed and affectively blunted. Her Paxil was increased to 40mg and trazodone was eventually added for sleep continuity disturbance. She was also treated with a number of therapies, appearing quite motivated for the program and without any particular withdrawal related symptoms. On 8/2/04, she was noted as affectively “neutral” and on 8/8/04, she conceded that she was “very guarded all her life.” On 8/13/04, her psychiatrist noted her as still “anxious about not having a very detailed and concrete plan for her recovery.”  However, by 8/15/04 she was noted as “cheerful and bright” and the remaining notes in her chart consistently point to her as such in mood and in affect. The patient remained in the chemical dependency treatment program until 8/27/04 and is seeking reimbursement for her stay. The Health Plan has denied coverage for chemical dependency treatment services from 7/31/04 through 8/27/04 indicating the patient could have been treated at a less intense level of care.The submitted records demonstrate the patient’s alcohol consumption was not only quite excessive on a daily basis for some years but was attendant with an increasing frequency of blackouts. All of this, superimposed on a highly avoidant character structure, would support the notion of her warranting residential treatment. Clearly, the patient did not have a great many immediate social supports to help her rein in her drinking and, in fact, she has tended to ward off connections with others. As such, outpatient treatment was not likely to be as effective as removing her from that environment, into one that was alcohol-free. As such, residential treatment was medically warranted. At the same time, the patient appears to have consistently brightened by 8/15/04 such that transfer thereafter to partial hospitalization would have been appropriate. Hence, I have determined that chemical dependency treatment services were medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition through 8/15/04. Accordingly, the Health Plan’s denial should be partially overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 43-year-old female with long-standing anorexia nervosa who was admitted to residential treatment on 11/11/04 due to notable obsessive concern about being fat, with concurrent caloric restriction. Admission weight was 103 pounds. She was treated with a number of therapies as well as medications. The patient was eventually stabilized on a regimen of Klonopin, Seroquel, Risperdal, and Zoloft. A very significant concurrent problem concerned obsessive rumination about possibly being sexually inappropriate with her young son. The noted medication regimen helped quite a bit in this regard.Notes from 12/29/04 indicate the patient stated, “I’m on a new medication and I feel that I have more control of the thoughts and can counteract them. I have less rumination and I’m following my meal plan.” Her therapist noted she focused on her abdomen being distended and feeling “fat” and was trying to get staff to comment on her abdomen.On 1/3/05, it was noted the patient’s weight had increased and she had progressed but remained fragile, and easily tearful because of irrational thoughts and beliefs that she has.On 1/12/05, it was noted the patient was pleasant, cooperative, and her affect was bright and she socialized with peers and staff most of the night. The patient stated she is now comfortable with what she eats. It was noted she ate 100% of her snack and tolerated it well without any distress.On 1/14/05, the patient stated, “I’m looking forward to going home,” and “I’ve learned to deal with my OCD thoughts and my rough times, the rough times are what helped me get through.” The patient was also noted as stating, “I am getting better, I can’t wait to be with my baby on discharge.” Her therapist noted her affect was brighter and her weight was 110 pounds. It was further reported the patient was still having obsessive-compulsive thoughts, but was handling them in a positive way.On 1/16/05, the patient discussed going to the outpatient program and stated, “I think I’m finally able to do it.” It was noted her affect was somewhat depressed but more realistic.On 1/17/05, the patient was interacting well with peers, participated in groups, was helpful with others, and eating 95% of her meals. The patient stated, “I am doing so much better.” It was noted she was compliant with the eating disorder program.On 1/18/05, the patient stated, “I’m looking forward to going into the partial program. I think it will be a good transition for me.” Her therapist noted the patient was quiet, calm and compliant and affect/mood was appropriate. The patient was making discharge plans, experiencing less obsessive-compulsive thoughts, and eating 100% of meals.On 1/19/05, the patient stated, “I am doing good. I like the program I’m working on.” Her therapist noted the patient looked alert and cheerful, and was sitting in the kitchen eating apple pie with a cup of hot cocoa. Her affect was appropriate.The patient has requested reimbursement for residential treatment services received from 1/18/05 through 1/22/05. The Health Plan has denied the request on the basis the services at issue were not medically necessary.Though this patient suffered from a number of problems including anorexia nervosa, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and depression, she clearly improved quite a bit by 1/18/05. The clinical notes provided do not include any evidence of a significant level of morbidity by 1/18/05. In fact, notes from 1/19/05 indicate the patient looked alert and cheerful, and was eating apple pie with a cup of hot cocoa. Hence, the submitted evidence demonstrates the patient could have been managed at a lower level of care as of 1/18/05. As such, I have determined the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The patient is a 47-year-old female who was admitted to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) following an auto versus pedestrian accident, which occurred on 11/24/04. She was admitted to skilled care on 12/6/04 and discharged on 12/17/04. The patient reached contact guard assist (CGA) with physical therapy on 12/14/04. At that time, she was also CGA with toileting and LB bathing. She continues to receive physical therapy at home. There is no evidence that her home environment was assessed as safe and accessible. The patient has requested authorization for additional SNF services. The Health Plan has denied the request indicating the submitted documentation does not demonstrate additional SNF services are medically necessary. Inpatient rehabilitation is provided to patients who have care needs that cannot be met in the home. The submitted evidence indicates the patient was sent home in a dependent state. There is no evidence that at the time of discharge appropriate services were in place to meet the patient’s care needs. The patient had not met her maximum rehabilitation potential at the time of discharge and she could have benefited from continued rehabilitation services. Based upon the documentation provided, it is unclear what services the patient requires at this time. Therefore, I have determined the Health Plan’s denial should be upheld at this time. However, the Health Plan should provide a full home health care evaluation to determine the type of care the patient requires.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is an 85-year-old female who was transferred to a SNF following hospitalization for treatment of pneumonia. In addition, the patient had multiple comorbidities including dementia and functional decline. While in the SNF, the patient received skilled physical and occupational therapy from 6/1/04 to 6/16/04. The patient made minimal gains during this time period except in endurance. Endurance training does require receipt of services from skilled personnel. The patient remained in the SNF until 7/8/04. The Health Plan has denied coverage for the services the patient received from 6/18/04 to 7/8/04. The patient did not make any clinically significant gains after 6/1/04. Skilled rehabilitation services are provided with the goal of enabling a patient to reach maximum functional status. Once maximum functional status is reached, it is reasonable to provide continued endurance training at a non-skilled level. The records provided demonstrate the patient had reached maximum functional status by 6/1/04 and there was no indication that continued therapy would benefit the patient’s condition. In fact, the records provided demonstrate the continued therapy did not increase the patient’s functional level. Therefore, I have determined the services at issue were not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 51-year-old female with left acetabular posterior wall fracture, right ankle fracture, odontoid process fracture, and right wrist fracture. She was transferred to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) on 11/24/04 for physical therapy to improve transfer. She is non-weight bearing in both lower extremities and has a halo device. The records indicate non-weight bearing of right lower extremity is to continue through 1/13/05. The patient has been recommended for restorative nursing activity as of 12/10/04. She wishes to receive additional SNF services. The Heath Plan has determined further SNF services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. Review of the submitted clinical information indicates the patient does not meet medical necessity criteria for SNF services. There is insufficient evidence that the requested services are likely to provide benefit and restoration of function. Patients such as this patient (i.e., non-weight bearing status) generally undergo limited rehabilitation courses until their orthopedic issues resolve. Based upon the information provided, the patient’s injuries preclude significant benefit from physical therapy until her bones are able to tolerate weight bearing. Therefore, I have determined that the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 58-year-old obese woman with a fracture to her right ankle. She has had some progress with physical therapy, particularly with bed mobility. However, the patient has not progressed with transfer and still requires two-person transfer. Based upon the submitted information, the patient’s progress with parallel bars is not clear. The patient has requested authorization and coverage for continued daily inpatient skilled therapy. The Health Plan has denied her request on the basis the requested therapy is not medically necessary.The submitted documentation does not provide compelling evidence the patient has reached her skilled rehabilitation plateau. Although the patient did not progress with transfer ability, there is evidence she progressed slowly but consistently with occupational therapy. There is potential for continued benefit in this case, particularly if the patient has been able to progress with parallel bars. In the absence of evidence the patient has plateaued with occupational therapy, continued daily inpatient skilled therapy is medically indicated. Therefore, I have determined that the requested therapy is medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be overturned. The patient should be fully re-evaluated in two weeks to determine if continued daily skilled inpatient rehabilitation therapy is indicated.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 64-year-old female with diabetes who is currently on dialysis. The patient has experienced decreased mobility and ability to ambulate.  She was admitted to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) on 5/12/04. The submitted notes indicate the patient does well with physical therapy on days when she does not have dialysis but is too fatigued on days when she has dialysis to fully participate in physical therapy. A request has been made for continued SNF services. The Health Plan has denied the request on the basis that SNF services were not medically necessary after 6/13/04.The submitted records indicate the patient progressed from maximum assistance with bed mobility to standby assistance in a period of one month. Additionally, there is evidence the patient progressed from moderate assistance with ambulation to contact guard assistance within one month. Thus, the submitted medical records demonstrate the patient’s condition was improving with therapy. Furthermore, though it was noted the patient had trouble with physical therapy on days she had dialysis, there is no evidence that an attempt was made to schedule the patient’s physical therapy sessions in the morning followed by dialysis in the afternoon. Given the patient’s documented progress additional SNF services are medically appropriate and indicated.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 50-year-old female who experienced traumatic brain injury as the result of a fall from a horse in May 2004. In addition, the patient was previously diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Following the injury the patient received neurobehavioral rehabilitation services on a 14-day referral. The patient was subsequently readmitted to residential care. The patient remains severely impaired. The patient’s representative has requested authorization and coverage for additional neurobehavioral cognitive services. The Health Plan has denied authorization for the requested services on the basis that additional neurobehavioral cognitive services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition.Review of the submitted materials indicates the patient’s rehabilitation team believes the patient is appropriate for discharge to outpatient therapy and no longer requires inpatient rehabilitation. The patient did not make significant gains as a result of previous neurobehavioral cognitive services. There is no evidence that additional neurobehavioral cognitive services are likely to result in improvement in the patient’s cognitive abilities. Ongoing outpatient rehabilitation services appear to be medically appropriate. Therefore, I have determined that the requested services are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. The Health Plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient is a 26-year-old male with complete T12 spinal cord injury. The patient’s family is requesting inpatient rehabilitation therapy. The submitted information includes no evidence of a physician request for inpatient services. Recently, the patient was noted to be independent with catheterizations, pressure relief, and upper extremity dressings. On 4/1/04, it was noted the patient required minimal assistance with lower extremity dressing. Upon discharge from the hospital, it was noted the patient required minimal assistance with self-care except for shower transfers. The physical therapy evaluation of 3/27/04 indicated the patient required moderate assistance for bed mobility, supine to sit, and toilet. The patient apparently needed assistance to get his legs off bed for sliding board transfer. The patient appears to be safe at home with assistance from caregivers. A request has been made for inpatient rehabilitation therapy. The Health Plan has denied the request on the basis that additional inpatient therapy is not medically necessary.An inpatient rehabilitation program is not medically necessary for the patient to achieve goals of independent function. The patient appears to be safe at home with assistance from caregivers. It is not necessary that the patient be independent to be a candidate for in-home rehabilitation therapy. It is only necessary that the patient’s caregivers be able to safely care for him. With continued in-home or outpatient rehabilitation therapy the patient is likely to achieve independence with transfers and bed mobility. Based upon the information set forth above, I have determined that the requested therapy is not medically necessary. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial should be upheld. However, based upon the submitted records it appears the patient requires a more intensive in-home rehabilitation program than he has been receiving.  The patient should receive at least three hours a day of in-home rehabilitation therapy with a dedicated team approach to therapy. The outpatient day treatment previously recommended by the Health Plan would be a safe and appropriate alternative.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: The patient has complete spinal cord injury and tertraplegia due to hyperextension of his neck after a fall. He received two courses of inpatient acute rehabilitation therapy in a skilled nursing facility (SNF). He progressed well in the second acute hospital-based rehabilitation, probably because he had made some neurologic recovery. He was discharged to another SNF on 2/6/04. A request has been made for continued inpatient rehabilitation services. The Health Plan has denied the request on the basis that the requested services are not medically necessary.Review of the information provided demonstrates that the patient no longer required acute inpatient rehabilitation therapy as of 2/6/04. However, it appears the patient’s course of rehabilitation ended abruptly upon transfer to another SNF. Though the patient was near the end of his rehabilitation program he had not completed the program. Based on the submitted evidence, as of 2/6/04 the patient required daily skilled inpatient rehabilitation therapy for a period of four weeks. Furthermore, outpatient therapy was not indicated at that time as there was no appropriate discharge planning in place for the patient.Therefore, I have determined that daily skilled inpatient rehabilitation therapy was medically necessary after 2/6/04. As such, the Health Plan’s denial should be partially overturned. Given the length of time since the cessation of inpatient rehabilitation therapy, the patient should undergo an evaluation at his current SNF to determine his capabilities with the environment and to ascertain whether he is at maximum potential. If the examining provider determines that additional inpatient rehabilitation therapy is medically indicated, the patient should receive four weeks of daily skilled inpatient rehabilitation therapy. However, at that time, the patient should be reevaluated by his physician to determine if further skilled inpatient rehabilitation therapy is needed.

The health plan denied the request indicating there are no contracted providers in the enrollee’s location.  The Review Organization's Physician Consultant examined the medical records submitted and determined twelve hours of skilled care is sufficient and consistent with his chronic and stable respiratory status.  Therefore, the health plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Home Health Care
Findings: The mother of a 6-month-old male requested home skilled nursing care for treatment of myofibrillar myopathy.  The health plan denied the request indicating the services are not medically necessary.  The Review Organization's Physician Consultant examined the medical records submitted and determined a child dependent on a ventilator and requiring gastrostomy feedings, skilled nursing care is a medical necessity, not “assistance in the activities of daily living,” as noted by the health plan.  The option of placing this child, who has a family willing to provide care at home, into a skilled nursing facility is not medically appropriate.  Therefore, the health plan’s denial should be overturned.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
Findings: A 56-year-old male requested inpatient rehabilitation therapy (skilled nursing facility level of care) following rotator cuff surgery. The health plan denied the request indicating the requested services are not medically necessary as the enrollee can safely and effectively be treated at a less intense level of care. The Review Organization's Physician Consultant examined the medical records submitted and determined there is potential the enrollee will require a period of skilled care post-operatively, however, the consultant found that the health plan is correct that the level and duration of care cannot be assessed pre-operatively.  Therefore, the health plan’s denial should be upheld.

Treatment Category: Rehabilitation Services - Skilled Nursing Facility - Inpatient
